section.content: 本文描述了用于主动机器学习的技术。一种主动机器学习方法可以包括：通过主动机器学习系统发起主动机器学习，主动机器学习系统被配置为对辅助机器学习模型进行训练，以产生至少一个新的被标记的观察；基于主动机器学习改善目标机器学习模型的容量；以及在改善目标机器学习模型的容量之后，利用至少一个新的被标记的观察重新训练辅助机器学习模型。另外，根据本文提供的描述，目标机器学习模型是有限容量的机器学习模型。

Techniques for active machine learning are described herein. An active machine learning method may include: initiating active machine learning by an active machine learning system configured to train an auxiliary machine learning model to generate at least one new tagged observation; improving the capacity of the target machine learning model based on active machine learning; and retraining the auxiliary machine learning model with the at least one new labeled observation after improving the capacity of the target machine learning model. In addition, according to the description provided herein, the target machine learning model is a limited capacity machine learning model.

Active machine learningBackground

Machine learning generally includes the construction or generation of machine learning algorithms that can learn from data. These algorithms are used to build models for generating a classifier for a specific purpose based on features. Active machine learning is a method by which a "teacher" (e.g., user) provides training samples to train functions of a model.

Historically, whether training samples were marked or unmarked was based on a particular purpose. For example, in existing systems, training samples for implementing a classifier that classifies documents related to the topic of baseball typically include document samples that are marked as related to baseball and document samples that are marked as unrelated to baseball.

Other existing training samples are unlabeled. For example, an unlabeled sample may or may not be related to baseball. Thus, a third party (e.g., teacher) must mark existing unlabeled training samples so that the model has valuable input through which to learn the associated functions.

In particular, active learning requires a relatively high quality labeled training sample so that the model can learn the desired function sufficiently for future classification of any number of unlabeled input documents. However, it is often costly to find high quality labeled training examples available for machine learning algorithms in a virtually unlimited number of unlabeled documents. For example, many users are employed to interpret unlabeled documents to determine feasibility for machine learning purposes. However, if a particular model trained by existing machine learning algorithms needs to be limited, the feasibility of each possible candidate for a labeled training sample must be considered even more carefully and the cost may exceed the desired goal.

Disclosure of Invention

The techniques discussed herein facilitate active machine learning by incrementally characterizing a target machine learning model with an auxiliary machine learning model. The auxiliary machine learning model may be a machine learning model having a relatively large range compared to the target machine learning model.

The above-described aspects may also be implemented as a computer control apparatus, a computer process, a computing system, or as an article of manufacture such as a computer storage medium. This summary is provided to introduce a selection of concepts in a simplified form that are further described below in the detailed description. This summary is not intended to identify key features or essential features of the claimed subject matter, nor is it intended to be used to limit the scope of the claimed subject matter. The term "technology" can refer, for example, to systems, methods, computer-readable media, computer-executable instructions, modules, algorithms, hardware logic (e.g., field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs), application Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs), application Specific Standard Products (ASSPs), systems-on-a-chip (SOCs), complex Programmable Logic Devices (CPLDs)), and/or the above-described contexts and techniques allowed throughout this document. Furthermore, the claimed subject matter is not limited to examples of implementations that solve any or all disadvantages noted in any part of this disclosure.

Drawings

The specific embodiments are described with reference to the accompanying drawings. In the figures, the leftmost digit(s) of a reference number identifies the figure in which the reference number first appears. The same reference numbers in different drawings identify similar or identical items.

FIG. 1 is a diagram illustrating aspects of several components provided by an exemplary operating environment and techniques described herein.

FIG. 2 is a flow chart illustrating aspects of one exemplary method for active machine learning described herein.

FIG. 3 is a flow chart illustrating aspects of one exemplary method described herein for active machine learning including selecting unlabeled observations with diversity.

FIG. 4 is a flow diagram illustrating aspects of one exemplary method for active machine learning described herein that includes accounting for output from both an auxiliary machine learning model and a target machine learning model.

FIG. 5 illustrates a graph depicting output scores and associated subset token sets for implementing diversity of choices for unlabeled observations of an exemplary auxiliary machine learning model described herein.

Fig. 6 is a computer architecture diagram illustrating an exemplary computer hardware and software architecture.

Detailed Description

SUMMARY

The following detailed description is directed to techniques for active machine learning that may be provided by a software product or a set of software products. The techniques presented herein facilitate relatively accurate identification of high quality training samples for use in active machine learning algorithms or associated models. Furthermore, the techniques may improve the efficiency of training a limited capacity model. Furthermore, the techniques may facilitate incremental characterization for limited capacity models to achieve accurate and desired output from classifiers created by the limited capacity models.

As used herein, the phrase "limited capacity model" and variants thereof refer to machine learning models that are limited or restricted in capacity. One exemplary limited capacity model is a machine learning model having a limited number of features. However, the features may include positive features and negative features. Another exemplary limited capacity model is a machine learning model in which the total number of n-grams sought (e.g., words or word tuples sought in a document) is limited or restricted. The limited capacity model allows deployment of classifiers that are also limited in size to achieve gain in memory efficiency. In addition, transmitting a limited capacity model and/or a classifier that is also limited in size may reduce network traffic in a mobile network, for example, when transmitting the classifier and/or model to a mobile device for deployment.

As used herein, the phrase "achromatopsia" and variants thereof refer to the lack of ability of the target machine learning model to distinguish between individual or different observations, although these different observations differ in the manner of definition. For example, a classifier trained in a target machine learning model may be "achromatopsia" for the differences between a web page describing a birdcage and a web page describing a batting cage. However, the same classifier may not be "achromatopsia" for the distinction between advertising for baseball bats and advertising related to the museum presentation of winged bats.

As used herein, the phrase "diversity" and variations thereof refer to the existence of a number of differences between the individual observations of a collection of observations in the collection. For example, a diverse set of observations includes a diversity across many or all of the observations contained therein.

As mentioned briefly above, features are components of the machine learning model described herein. The term "feature" and variants thereof refer to data contained in a machine learning model. Examples of features include words, phrases, n-grams, and lexicographical data. Additionally, as used herein, the phrase "incremental characterization" and variations thereof refers specifically to adding or removing features from a target machine learning model in an incremental manner. In contrast, conventional machine learning techniques typically add multiple features or manipulate a machine learning model in a non-incremental manner.

In general, techniques for active machine learning described herein include active machine learning based on a second auxiliary machine learning model, training a target machine learning model by incrementally characterizing and/or by improving the capacity of the target machine learning model. The auxiliary machine learning model may have infinite capacity or may have a relatively large capacity compared to the target machine learning model. The active machine learning system may utilize active machine learning of the auxiliary machine learning model to identify a range of achromatopsia of the target machine learning model. Thereafter, after the range of achromates is identified, a new high quality labeled training sample may be generated and used to determine the features to be added or removed from the target machine learning model. The achromatopsia of the target machine learning model, its scope, and other attributes are described more fully below with reference to the accompanying drawings.

Implementing diversity in active machine learning of an auxiliary machine learning model can at least partially improve the efficiency of the techniques described herein. For example, the active machine learning system may select a new unlabeled view that is diverse across all selected unlabeled views. In this way, the active machine learning system can assemble a higher quality training set. The diversity may be achieved in a number of different ways, which will be described more fully below with reference to fig. 5.

As discussed in additional detail above, a software product or set of software products may provide some or all of the functionality described herein that involves active machine learning. For example, network services may be deployed through a service provider network (e.g., with an operating system and/or application programs). The web service may allow third parties to use the techniques described herein for training limited capacity machine learning models based on active machine learning with relatively large capacity auxiliary machine learning models. The network services may be deployed across one or more host processors, computers, servers, or other computer hardware and may be provided via one or more network connections. In addition, according to at least one example, knowledge relating to the size and attributes of the marked training observations may be stored or maintained at the service provider network. Thus, if desired, a new classifier can be built on the pre-labeled data, reducing the construction cost compared to implementing the new classifier from the head.

While the subject matter described herein is presented in the general context of program modules that execute in conjunction with an operating system and application programs executing on a computer system, those skilled in the art will recognize that other examples may be implemented in combination with other types of program modules. Generally, program modules include routines, programs, components, data structures, and other types of structures that perform particular tasks or implement particular abstract data types. Moreover, those skilled in the art will appreciate that the techniques described herein may be practiced with various computer system configurations, including single-processor or multiprocessor systems, single-core or multi-core processors, microprocessor-based or programmable consumer electronics, hand-held computing devices, minicomputers, personal computers, mainframe computers, combinations thereof, and the like.

In the following detailed description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and which illustrate specific examples by way of illustration.

Exemplary Environment

FIG. 1 illustrates aspects of an exemplary operating environment 100 that includes several components provided by the techniques described herein. The environment 100 of fig. 1 includes one or more untagged observations pool 102 within which are disposed a plurality of untagged observations 104. Untagged observations 104 may alternatively be dispersed across multiple different pools or other devices/components not specifically shown in fig. 1.

In machine learning, classification is a problem of identifying which category in a collection of categories (e.g., sub-populations, categories, etc.) a new observation belongs to based on a training data set that contains observations for which the member category is known or has been labeled. In general, unlabeled observations 104 are observations that the particular class or category of member is unknown. The categories may include any number of categories based on any desired attributes. For example, the categories may include "SPAM messages," "web pages," "baseball documents," or any other category. Accordingly, the description provided herein should not be limited to a particular category or type of category, but should be understood to encompass any suitable category or category of observations.

The environment 100 includes one or more marked observation pools 106 within which a plurality of marked observations 108 are disposed. Tagged view 108 may alternatively be dispersed across many different pools 106 or other devices/components not specifically shown in fig. 1 in a similar manner as described with respect to untagged view 104.

In general, a tagged view is a view of which the particular class or category of member is known. The marked observations may include metadata associated therewith that particularly recalls the associated category, a binary representation of whether it belongs to the category (e.g., a "yes/no" tag), and/or other forms of marked observations and associated storage of the mark.

The environment 100 includes an active machine learning system 110 in operative communication with the untagged observation pool 102 and the tagged observation pool 106. Such active communication may occur over a network or other communication medium that can facilitate communication and transfer of information between the active machine learning system 110 and the untagged observation pool 102 and/or the tagged observation pool 106.

In some examples, the active machine learning system 110 may be implemented as one or more components, such as software modules executing on one or more processors in one or more computations. In various examples, the active machine learning system 110 may be implemented as discrete components having hardware and software associated therewith for implementing some or all of the functions described herein. In addition, other examples include virtualization of the active machine learning system 110 on the service provider network described above, distribution of computer-executable instructions configured to direct a processor to implement the active machine learning system 110, and other suitable implementations.

The active machine learning system 110 may include an auxiliary machine learning model 112 and a target machine learning model 114. The auxiliary machine learning model 112 may include any desired model having a relatively large capacity as compared to the target machine learning model 114. In at least one example, the auxiliary machine learning model 112 is a bag of words machine learning model that uses the frequency of occurrence of each word in a bag of words as a feature for training a classifier. In some examples, the auxiliary machine learning model 112 is a semantic machine learning model or a classifier similar to a bag of words model that can have basic features of infinite or substantially infinite capacity. Other examples of the auxiliary machine learning model 112 are possible. The target machine learning model 114 is a limited capacity model as defined above.

As shown in fig. 1, an active learning routine configured to train the auxiliary machine learning model 112 to learn a desired function selects unlabeled observations 116 of the test specimen. Thereafter, the auxiliary machine learning model 112 may generate outputs for interpretation by the comparison component 118, the labeling component 120, and the characterization component 122. For example, the comparison component 118 can pass the score generated by the auxiliary machine learning model 112 to the tagging component 120 and the characterization component 122.

When a score is received, the tagging component 120 may convert the untagged observations 116 of the specimen into new tagged observations 124 based on the received score. The tagging component 120 may then cause the new tagged observations 124 to be stored in the tagged observation pool 106 for training the auxiliary machine learning model 112.

Additionally, when a score is received, the characterization component 122 can identify possible features 126 to add or remove from the target machine learning model 114 based on the score. The capacity improvement component 128 can process the possible features 126 to determine features 130 to be incrementally added or removed from the target machine learning model 114.

It should be appreciated that the capacity improving member 128 may take any suitable form. According to at least one example, the capacity improving component 128 includes a user interface for accepting input selecting a feature 130 from the possible features 126. According to other examples, the capacity improving component 128 may include a method for automatically selecting the feature 130 from the possible features 126.

In addition, the comparing component 118, the marking component 120, and the characterizing component 122 can be implemented in a number of different forms. The specific operation of each of the comparing component 118, the labeling component 120, and the characterizing component 122 will be described more fully with reference to fig. 2-4.

According to at least one example, the target machine learning model 114 is also capable of receiving unlabeled observations 116 of the specimen selected through active machine learning of the auxiliary machine learning model 112. Thereafter, the target machine learning model 114 may generate a second score representing the unlabeled observations 116 of the process sample such that the comparison component 118 is capable of comparing the first score from the auxiliary machine learning model 112 to the second score from the target machine learning model 114 to determine a likelihood that the target machine learning model has generated a false positive or false negative result or error. Thus, the tagging component 120 and the characterization component 122 can take into account the likelihood to generate better possible features 126 and generate new tagged observations 124 of quality.

Exemplary procedure

A more detailed description of the functionality of the active machine learning system 110 and associated components is provided later with reference to fig. 2-4. Although described as occurring sequentially, it should be understood that any of the operations of the individual methods described below may be processed in parallel and that some operations may be omitted in some circumstances without departing from the techniques described herein.

FIG. 2 is a flow diagram illustrating aspects of one exemplary method 200 for active machine learning in accordance with at least one example. The method 200 of active machine learning may include: at block 202, an active learning process is initiated using the auxiliary machine learning model 112. For example, the active machine learning system 110 may direct the auxiliary machine learning model 112 to select unlabeled observations 116 of one or more specimens for processing and outputting scores. The characterization component 122 can process the score.

Thereafter, at block 204, the characterization component 122 may improve the capacity of the target machine learning model based on the score. For example, based on the scores from the auxiliary machine learning model 112, the characterization component 122 may determine that one or more possible features 126 should be added or removed from the target machine learning model, e.g., highest score, lowest score, scores within a defined range, etc. In general, the score indicates whether an unlabeled observation of a sample belongs to or does not belong to a particular class. Thus, if the score indicates that the unlabeled observations belong to a category, one or more possible features 126 may be extracted from the labeled observations (e.g., labeled observations 132) for training a target machine learning model to identify similar unlabeled observations as belonging to the category. If the score indicates that the unlabeled observations do not fall within a category, one or more possible features 126 may be extracted from the labeled observations 132 for training the target machine learning model to identify similar unlabeled observations as not falling within the category. Based on these possible features 126, the capacity improvement component 118 can improve the capacity of the target machine learning model 114 by incrementally adding features 130 to the target machine learning model 114/removing features 130 from the target machine learning model 114.

After improving the capacity of the target machine learning model 114, the method 200 further includes: at block 206, the auxiliary machine learning model is retrained with the marked observations 132. For example, the active machine learning system 110 may provide a new tagged observation 124 and one or more tagged observations 132 from the tagged observation pool 106 to maintain or modify the auxiliary machine learning model 112. Because the capacity of the auxiliary machine learning model 112 is not limited, retraining the auxiliary machine learning model 112 can improve the quality of the labeled training set of target machine learning models 114 without affecting the capacity of the target machine learning model 114.

As shown in FIG. 2, the method 200 may iterate through blocks 202-206 to incrementally improve the capacity of the target machine learning model 114 and retrain the auxiliary machine learning model 112 based on the newly tagged observations 124. This incremental improvement allows the limited capacity of the target machine learning model 114 to be maintained within desired limits or constraints. For example, it may be desirable to maintain a particular range limit on the overall number of features contained within the target machine learning model 114 to produce a compact classifier. In this case, the method 200 may facilitate compactness of the classifier based on the incremental nature of the added and removed features of the target machine learning model 114.

The selection of a set of unlabeled observations 116 of a diverse sample by the auxiliary machine learning model 112 can result in a higher quality target machine learning model 114 and/or at least partial gain in the efficiency of training the target machine learning model 114. For example, a diverse set of observations may include a diversity across many or all of the observations contained therein.

FIG. 3 is a flow diagram illustrating aspects of one exemplary method 300 for active machine learning including selecting unlabeled observations with diversity according to at least one example. The method 300 comprises the following steps: at block 302, the auxiliary machine learning model 112 selects unlabeled observations 116 of one or more specimens.

The auxiliary machine learning model 112 may select unlabeled observations 116 of one or more specimens such that the labeled observation pool 106 is diverse. For example, unlabeled observations 116 of a specimen may be selected by the auxiliary machine learning model 112 such that they are diversified across all selected unlabeled observations. In this way, a higher quality training set of marked observations 108 can be assembled.

The auxiliary machine learning model 112 may implement diversity in selecting unlabeled observations 116 of the specimen in a variety of ways. According to one example, the auxiliary machine learning model 112 may implement one or more functions, referred to as secondary modulus functions, for selecting unlabeled observations 116 of a new specimen. According to another example, the auxiliary machine learning model 112 may determine a subset marking set, e.g., from the marked observations 132, wherein selecting from the subset marking set provides a guarantee of at least a minimum level of diversity. Both the secondary modulo function for diversity and the threshold-based method for determining the subset mark set will be described more fully with reference to fig. 5.

Returning to FIG. 3, at block 304, the tagging component 120 may convert the untagged observations 116 of one or more samples into new tagged observations 124. In some examples, the converting may include: the marking component 120 selects the unlabeled observations 116 of one or more samples. Thereafter, at block 306, the capacity improvement component 128 may improve the target machine learning model 114. At block 308, the auxiliary machine learning model 112 of the active machine learning system 110 may undergo retraining. In some examples, the improvements and retraining described in blocks 306 and 308 are substantially similar to the improvements and retraining described above with reference to blocks 204 and 206, respectively. Accordingly, similar details are omitted herein for the sake of brevity.

As shown in FIG. 3, the method 300 may iterate through blocks 302-308 to incrementally improve the capacity of the target machine learning model 114 based on new tagged observations obtained during retraining of the auxiliary machine learning model 112. In this example, the newly marked observations may be based on a diverse set of unmarked observations. Thus, incremental improvements to the target machine learning model 114 may be based on more varied outputs from the auxiliary machine learning model 112, and fewer improvement operations or iterations may be applied than conventional approaches.

As briefly described above, the active machine learning system 110 may also operate to allow the target machine learning model 114 to provide output for comparison and further improve the features contained therein. FIG. 4 is a flow diagram illustrating aspects of one exemplary method 400 for active machine learning that includes considering output from an auxiliary machine learning model and a target machine learning model, in accordance with at least one example.

The method 400 includes: at block 402, the auxiliary machine learning model 112 selects unlabeled observations 116 of the specimen. The particular unlabeled observations may be selected from the unlabeled observations 104, for example, because it is not known which of the multiple categories the unlabeled observations belong to.

Thereafter, the method 400 includes: at block 404, a first score is assigned to untagged observations using the auxiliary machine learning model 112. Further, the method 400 may include: at block 406, a second score is assigned to the untagged observations using the target machine learning model 114.

At block 408, the comparison component 118 compares the first score with the second score to determine a likelihood that the target machine learning model 114 will return a false positive or false negative result. In some examples, the comparison component 118 compares the first score and the second score as the first score and the second score are assigned by the auxiliary machine learning model 112 and the target machine learning model 114, respectively.

In general, the comparison may include determining the magnitude of the difference between the first score and the second packet. Thereafter, the comparison component 118 can determine that the target machine learning model 114 has returned a false positive when the magnitude is negative. Additionally, the positive magnitude comparison component 118 can determine that the target machine learning model 114 has returned a false negative.

It should be appreciated that by identifying false positive and false negative results, the range of achromatopsia of the target machine learning model 114 becomes clear. For example, it may be rare that the auxiliary machine learning model 112 and the target machine learning model 114 are "inconsistent" and represent false positives and false negatives. In these examples, the cause of the false positive or false negative may provide valuable information regarding the limitations or "achromatopsia" of the limited capacity target machine learning model 114. This information may be maintained for use by the characterization component 122 and the capacity improvement component 128 to achieve better accuracy through iterative improvement of the target machine learning model 114.

At block 410, based at least on the likelihood, the tagging component 120 converts the untagged observations 116 into new tagged observations 124. In some examples, the tagging component 120 performs the conversion after the comparison component 118 determines a likelihood of false positives or false negatives. Thus, the new marked observations 124 may represent samples of the gap that help at least partially narrow the achromatopsia of the target machine learning model 114.

Thereafter, at block 412, the characterization component 122 may determine the features 130 to be added or removed from the target machine learning model 114 based on the possible features 126. Possible features 126 may be tailored based on the comparison of blocks 408 and 410, and thus may also help narrow the gap of achromatopsia exposed by comparing the two outputs. The capacity improvement component 128 may then improve the target machine learning model 114 based on the features 130 at block 414.

Incremental improvements in the capacity of the target machine learning model 114 may include achieving diversity in the selection of unlabeled observations 116 and comparing the outputs from the auxiliary machine learning model 112 and the target machine learning model 114 to help determine how to correct achromatopsia. It should be appreciated that each of the above methods may be modified to include both concepts at any level of granularity. For example, the diversity of choices from method 300 may be implemented in one or both of methods 200 and 400. Similarly, the determination in method 400 may be implemented in one or both of methods 200 and 300 to assist in disagreement between machine learning model 112 and target machine learning model 114. In accordance with these methods, exemplary individual details relating to implementing selection diversity in any of the above-described methods will be described with reference to FIG. 5.

The graph of the exemplary curve 502 shown in fig. 5 depicts output scores of one or more auxiliary machine learning models and associated subset marking sets 504 for achieving diversity in unlabeled observation choices in accordance with at least one example. Curve 502 represents the output of the auxiliary machine learning model 112 based on the observation pool (e.g., pools 102 and/or 106).

As shown in fig. 5, the y-axis of curve 502 represents the number of observations in the observation pool. For example, a pool of observations related to selection diversity is generally understood to be untagged observations, e.g., untagged observations 104. However, in some examples, selecting a diverse training set that includes marked observations 108 is also applicable. The x-axis of curve 502 generally represents the score output from the auxiliary machine learning model 112. For example, the score may be a normalized score between 0 and 1.

As further shown in the example of fig. 5, as the number of observations increases, the score decreases. In addition, as the number of observations decreases (or if only diverse choices of observations are made), the score increases. Thus, a subset of marked sets of unmarked observations may be identified for a particular one or more observation pools. Thereafter, the auxiliary machine learning model 112 may be configured to select unlabeled observations of the specimen from only the subset of labeled sets to increase diversity in the unlabeled specimens.

As briefly mentioned above, the subset mark set may be based on a sub-modulo function or on the implementation of a threshold-based method. Other examples are also possible.

With respect to the threshold-based approach, the threshold 506 may be selected such that the desired score is 0.5 or greater. Thereafter, sampling is performed only in the subset mark set, and samples are uniformly selected. After receiving feedback (e.g., by comparison component 118) of the actual score for the sample that is not observed with the marker, the threshold may be automatically calibrated to maintain the expected score of 0.5 or greater. Thus, a threshold of 0.5 may be automatically calibrated along the x-axis, such that different values of the threshold are possible.

Regarding the implementation of the secondary modulo function, the auxiliary machine learning model 112 is configured to select a set of untagged observations for subsequent tagging. Generally, a subset of unlabeled items (U_f) is filtered given a current classifier trained based on the auxiliary machine learning model 112. The subset U f should be filtered to include an equal number of positive and negative observations. After filtering the subset u_f, two secondary modulo functions are defined. The first order function is used for facility location (facility location) and is represented by equation 1 as follows:

equation 1: f (X) = \sum\i\in u_f } \max\j\in X } s\ij }

In equation 1, s_ { ij } is the similarity between observation i and observation j. The second order modulo function is a feature-based function and is represented by equation 2 below:

equation 2: f (X) = \sum\i\in F } \log m_f (X)

In equation 2, m_f (j) =observe TF-IDF score of feature f in j.

One round of unlabeled observation selection includes solving the optimization problem represented by equation 3 given below:

equation 3: max_ { x\subsetequ_f, |x|\leqb } f (x\cup L)

In at least one example, each round of unlabeled observation choices includes solving the optimization problem represented by equation 3. In some examples, at least one round of unlabeled observation selection is performed when defining the secondary modulo function. In equation 3, L is the set of marked observations. Thus, as described above, at least two ways of implementing diversity for selecting unlabeled observations have been proposed herein. However, additional examples with different schemes are also applicable.

It should be appreciated that the logical operations described above can be implemented (1) as a sequence of computer implemented acts or program modules running on a computing system, and/or (2) as interconnected machine logic circuits or circuit modules within the computing system. The implementation is a matter of choice dependent on the performance and other requirements of the computing system. Accordingly, the logical operations described herein are referred to variously as state operations, acts or modules. The operations, acts and/or modules may be implemented in software, firmware, special purpose digital logic, hardware, and any combination thereof. It should also be understood that more or fewer operations may be performed than shown in the figures and described herein. These operations may also be performed in an order different than described herein.

Fig. 6 is an exemplary computer architecture showing a computer 600 capable of executing the software components described herein for active machine learning in the manner presented above. The computer architecture shown in fig. 6 illustrates an example computer system configuration, and the computer 600 may be used to perform any aspect of the components and/or modules presented herein that are described as being executed on or in communication with the active machine learning system 110.

The computer architecture shown in fig. 6 includes: a processing unit 602 (e.g., a central processing unit "CPU", a graphics processing unit "GPU", or other processing unit described herein); a computer-readable medium, which may include one or more system memories 608, including a random access memory 614 ("RAM") and a read only memory ("ROM") 616; and a system bus 604 that couples the memory to the processing unit 602. A basic input/output system containing the basic routines that help to transfer information between elements within the computer 600, such as during startup, is stored in the ROM 616. The computer 600 also includes a mass storage device 610 for storing an operating system 618, application programs, and other program modules, which will be described in greater detail below.

The mass storage device 610 is connected to the processing unit 602 through a mass storage controller (not shown) connected to the bus 604. The mass storage device 610 and its associated computer-readable media provide non-volatile storage for the computer 600. Although the description of computer-readable media contained herein refers to a mass storage device, such as a hard disk or CD-ROM drive, it should be appreciated by those skilled in the art that computer-readable media can include any available computer storage media or communication media that can be accessed by the computer 600.

Communication media may include computer readable instructions, data structures, program modules, or other data in a modulated data signal, such as a carrier wave. As used herein, the term "modulated data signal" means a signal that: one or more of its characteristics may be changed or set in such a manner as to encode information in the signal. By way of example, and not limitation, physical components that support the operation of a communication medium include: a wired medium such as a wired network or direct-wired connection; and wireless media such as acoustic, RF, infrared, and other wireless media. Combinations of any of the above should also be included within the scope of computer readable media.

By way of example, and not limitation, computer storage media may include volatile and nonvolatile, removable and non-removable media implemented in any method or technology for storage of information (e.g., computer readable instructions, data structures, program modules or other data). For example, computer storage media includes, but is not limited to, RAM, ROM, EPROM, EEPROM, flash memory or other memory technology, CD-ROM, digital versatile disks ("DVD"), HD-DVD, blu-ray, or other optical disk storage, magnetic cassettes, magnetic tape, magnetic disk storage or other magnetic storage devices, or any other medium which can be used to store the desired information and which can be accessed by computer 600. As used herein, "computer storage medium" does not include "communication medium".

According to various examples, computer 600 may operate in a networked environment using logical connections to remote computers through a network (e.g., network 620). The computer 600 may connect to the network 620 through a network interface unit 606 connected to the bus 604. It should be appreciated that the network interface unit 606 may also be utilized to connect to other types of networks and remote computer systems. The computer 600 may also include an input/output controller 612 for receiving and processing input from a number of other devices, including a keyboard, mouse, or electronic stylus, video camera, touch interface, and so forth. Similarly, an input/output controller may provide output to a display screen, a printer, or other type of output device.

As briefly described above, a number of program modules and data files may be stored in the mass storage device 610 and RAM 614 of the computer 600, including an operating system 618 suitable for controlling the operation of a network desktop, laptop, or server computer. The mass storage device 610 and the RAM 614 may also store one or more program modules, such as the auxiliary machine learning model 112, the target machine learning model 114, the comparison component 118, the tagging component 120, the characterization component 122, and/or the capacity improvement component 128 as described above. The mass storage device 610 and RAM 614 may also store other types of program modules, services, and data.
